x: ReaEdit is a free set of source-destination (S-D) editing tools for REAPER. Source-destination editing is the technique classical music engineers use to build a finished performance from many takes: you mark the passage you want to take (the source) and the place it should go (the destination), and one action makes the edit, with a crossfade at each join. It is how dedicated classical editing systems work, and ReaEdit brings it to an ordinary REAPER installation. ReaEdit is a small part of ReaClassical, the complete classical production system built on REAPER (recording, editing, mixing, mastering and rendering). It is made from the same S-D editing scripts, and it is yours to use free of charge for as long as you like. It needs no license key and no account. What you get: Source and destination IN and OUT markers, placed at the edit cursor The S-D edit itself: 2-, 3- and 4-point edits from whichever markers you have set, with automatic crossfades The assembly-line (3-point insert) edit for building a take from consecutive pieces A 4-point edit that time-stretches the source to fit the destination Delete with ripple, and delete leaving silence Editing between two open project tabs One key to open REAPER's crossfade editor, or, for screen reader users, a keyboard-driven crossfade mode Spoken feedback through OSARA, which is essential if you use a screen reader What you need: REAPER, plus ReaPack to install and update ReaEdit (or the zip download, which does not need ReaPack) No SWS, no ReaImGui, no other extensions If you are blind or low-vision, OSARA: it is what makes ReaEdit speak (the Accessibility FAQ explains how to install it) Where to start New to source-destination editing? Read Your First Edit next. Already comfortable with it? Skim Markers and Edit Types, then set up your keyboard shortcuts. ReaEdit does not assign any keyboard shortcuts for you, and it does not change how REAPER looks or behaves apart from the actions it adds. Everything here works in your existing REAPER setup.
ReaEdit is installed into an existing REAPER setup. There are two ways to get it. The recommended one is ReaPack, which registers the actions for you and keeps ReaEdit up to date.

Installing with ReaPack (recommended) ReaEdit has its own ReaPack repository, separate from ReaClassical's. Install ReaPack in REAPER if you do not have it yet. Choose Extensions > ReaPack > Import repositories..., paste https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chmaha/ReaClassical/main/ReaEdit/index.xml and press OK. Choose Extensions > ReaPack > Browse packages..., search for ReaEdit, right-click the package and choose Install, then press OK to apply. Open the Action List (Actions > Show action list...) and search for ReaEdit to find the actions. To update later, choose Extensions > ReaPack > Synchronize packages. ReaEdit is versioned separately from ReaClassical, starting at 1.0. Only the actions you use ReaPack adds just the 17 actions you use directly to your Action List. The keyboard crossfade mode is made of about 45 more small actions; they are installed, but they are not added to your Action List unless you set up the crossfade mode, which is only for OSARA users. If you do not use a screen reader you will never see them.

Installing from a zip (without ReaPack) Download ReaEdit.zip. Unzip it into REAPER's Scripts folder (Options > Show REAPER resource path in explorer/finder, then open Scripts). This creates a ReaEdit folder; keep all of its files together. In REAPER open the Action List, choose New action > Load ReaScript... and select Register ReaEdit actions.lua from the ReaEdit folder. Run it once: it adds every ReaEdit action to the Action List, and running it again is harmless. Search the Action List for ReaEdit and bind the shortcuts you want. A zip install is not updated automatically. To update, download the newest zip, unzip it over the old ReaEdit folder (allow it to overwrite) and run Register ReaEdit actions.lua again.
Removing ReaEdit With ReaPack, find ReaEdit in Browse packages, right-click it and choose Uninstall. With the zip, delete the ReaEdit folder and remove the leftover entries from the Action List.

Compatibility ReaEdit is tested with the version of REAPER that ships with ReaClassical (7.78 at the time of writing). Other recent versions are expected to work, but that is the one it is tested against. It needs no extensions: no SWS, no ReaImGui. If you are blind or low-vision, you should also install OSARA: it is what makes ReaEdit speak, and ReaEdit is built to be used with it. Using ReaClassical too? ReaEdit is for people who want S-D editing in their own REAPER. If you use ReaClassical, you already have these functions, with many more, so you do not need ReaEdit. Do not install ReaEdit into your ReaClassical instance. Keep ReaEdit for a separate, ordinary REAPER.

This walkthrough makes a complete source-destination edit. You need a project with some recorded material on one or more tracks: a take of a piece, and a second take of the same passage you would like to patch in. Anything will do for practice, even two copies of a short recording laid end to end. First, make sure the actions are easy to reach. Bind keyboard shortcuts to at least the four marker actions and S-D Edit (see Keyboard Shortcuts for suggestions). You can run everything from the Action List while you learn, but you will want keys very quickly.

The four steps Mark where the new material should go (destination). Put the edit cursor where the bad passage starts and run Add Destination IN marker. Move to where it ends and run Add Destination OUT Marker. Mark the good material you want to use (source). Put the cursor at the start of the good take and run Add Source IN marker. Move to the end and run Add Source OUT marker. Make the edit. Run S-D Edit. ReaEdit copies the material between the source markers, replaces the destination passage with it, closes up the gap and puts a short crossfade at each join. Listen. Play across both joins. If the edit is not right, undo it (one undo step) and adjust your markers. The markers are coloured so you can tell them apart at a glance: destination markers are cyan, source markers are green.

What just happened Every track was edited together. ReaEdit treats the tracks of a project as parallel channels of one recording, as you would have with several microphones, so the source passage came from all of them and went in on all of them. The four markers you placed are still there, so you can see exactly what was done. Placing a new marker of the same kind replaces the old one; see Markers. The crossfade length came from your preferences (35 ms to start with).
Next You do not always need all four markers: see Edit Types for 2- and 3-point edits, assembly-line editing and time-stretched edits. To remove a passage rather than replace it, see Deleting.

ReaEdit marks an edit with four markers. They are ordinary REAPER project markers, named and coloured by ReaEdit, so they show on the ruler and in the Region/Marker Manager like any other. Marker Name Colour Action Destination IN DEST-IN cyan Add Destination IN marker Destination OUT DEST-OUT cyan Add Destination OUT Marker Source IN SOURCE-IN green Add Source IN marker Source OUT SOURCE-OUT green Add Source OUT marker Destination is where the new material goes; source is where it comes from. IN is the start of a passage and OUT is its end.

Placing markers Each marker action puts its marker at the edit cursor, or at the play position if REAPER is playing, so you can place markers on the fly while listening. There is only ever one marker of each kind: placing a new SOURCE-IN removes the old one, in every open project tab. Each placement is its own undo step.

After an edit The markers you placed stay where they are, so you can see what was done, and you can undo and run the edit again with adjusted markers. If you set fewer than four markers, the missing ones that ReaEdit worked out for the edit (see Edit Types) are removed again once the edit is made, so they never get in your way.

Removing markers Delete All S-D markers removes the four markers from every open project. Delete S-D Project Markers removes the two project-tab markers (see Editing Between Project Tabs). Both are a single undo step. Marker numbers ReaEdit identifies its markers by their numbers (996 to 1001) as well as their names, so avoid using those numbers for markers of your own.
The S-D Edit action makes an edit from whichever of the four markers you have set. The more markers you set, the more control you have; the ones you leave out are worked out for you.

4-point edit Set all four markers. The source passage replaces the destination passage. If the two are different lengths, the material after the edit moves earlier or later (ripples) to fit. This is the most precise kind of edit and the one to reach for when you know exactly what you are replacing.

3-point edit Set any three markers. ReaEdit works out the fourth from the length of the pair you did set: Destination IN, source IN and source OUT: the source passage is placed at destination IN, and the destination OUT is calculated from the source length Destination IN, destination OUT and source IN: the source OUT is calculated from the destination length and so on for the other combinations Three-point editing is the everyday way to work: you say where it starts, what to use, and for how long.

2-point edit Set one destination marker and one source marker. ReaEdit fills in the missing ends from the ends of your material: Destination IN and source IN: from those points to the end of the source material and to the end of the project Destination OUT and source OUT: from the start of the material and of the project up to those points Source IN and destination OUT: from source IN to the end of the source, and from the start of the project to the destination OUT Source OUT and destination IN: from the start of the source to source OUT, and from destination IN to the end of the project Two-point edits are useful for quickly joining the start or end of one take to another.

Assembly line (3-point insert) 3-point Insert Edit builds a performance from consecutive pieces without replacing anything. Set destination IN, source IN and source OUT; the action inserts the source passage at destination IN and pushes everything after it later. When it has finished, it places a new destination IN at the end of the piece it just inserted, so the next piece follows straight on: set a new source IN and OUT and run the action again. Destination OUT is not needed, because it is worked out from the length of the source passage. ReaEdit remembers the item it just inserted. If you have moved destination IN away from the end of that item since the last assembly-line edit, it asks: Yes starts a new edit sequence at the marker where you put it No moves destination IN back to the edge of the last item, so you can continue the sequence Cancel does nothing

4-point edit with time-stretching Insert with timestretching needs all four markers (with fewer, nothing happens). It fits the source passage to the destination passage by stretching or shrinking it, which is handy for matching a short drop or a tempo difference. Use it sparingly: a large change will be audible. If there is no material between the source markers you will see "Please make sure there is material to copy between your source markers."

h: Crossfades, undo and what you will be told
x: Crossfades, undo and what you will be told Every edit puts a crossfade at each join, with a length set in Preferences. The whole edit is a single undo step. If ReaEdit had to shorten a crossfade because there was not enough source material, it tells you; with OSARA installed it speaks it, without OSARA it shows a message.

Two actions remove material rather than replacing it. Both use the source markers to say what to remove, so set SOURCE-IN and SOURCE-OUT first. If either is missing you will see "Please use SOURCE-IN and SOURCE-OUT markers".

Delete With Ripple Removes everything between the source markers, on every track, and closes the gap by moving the later material earlier, with a crossfade at the join. Use it to take out a cough, a repeat or a false start so the music simply carries on.

Delete Leaving Silence Removes the same material but leaves the gap where it was, so nothing else moves. Use it when timing must be preserved, for example while working on a section that is aligned to something else.

A tip for slivers After many rounds of zoomed-out editing it is easy to leave small, unwanted leftover pieces of earlier edits (slivers). Before an edit or a delete, ReaEdit clears slivers that sit right next to your markers so the join is clean, and tells you what it removed ("Removed sliver edit(s)"). It does not touch anything further away, so look at long projects occasionally.
ReaEdit puts a crossfade at every join it makes. The crossfade is written directly into the items, with a fixed length you choose, so the same edit always sounds the same.

Preferences Run Preferences (find it by searching the Action List for ReaEdit). There are three settings ("XFM" is the keyboard crossfade mode): S-D Crossfade length (ms) The length of the crossfade at each edit. Default = 35. Longer crossfades are smoother on sustained or reverberant material; shorter ones are better for fast passages. The crossfade mode's Reset action uses it too. XFM nudge (ms) How far each step moves in the keyboard crossfade mode: slipping, nudging, shifting, widening, narrowing and changing the fades. Default = 5. XFM x modifier multiplier The larger-step version of those keys moves this many times the nudge. Default = 5. The setting is saved with the project, so different projects can use different values.

When a crossfade is shortened If there is not enough source material to give a full crossfade at the source IN or OUT, the crossfade at that join is shortened to what is available, and ReaEdit tells you by how much, for example "Crossfade shortened to 12 ms at source-in due to limited source material." The edit is otherwise unaffected. If you want the full length, move the source marker a little further into the take.

Adjusting an edit afterwards Edits are ordinary REAPER items, so you can still trim, slip or fade them with REAPER's own tools, and undo takes the whole edit back in one step. To listen closely to a crossfade and fine-tune where it falls, use REAPER's own crossfade editor, described in REAPER's Crossfade Editor.

Screen reader users: use crossfade mode instead If you use OSARA, you do not need this window. It is visual, and it is not fully accessible with a screen reader at the moment. ReaEdit's keyboard-driven crossfade mode gives OSARA users full parity with the visual editor in the features classical music engineers use, driven entirely from the keyboard: moving the crossfade and the audio inside it, widening and narrowing it, shaping the fades, listening to each side and putting it back as it was, with every step spoken. The same Crossfade Editor action starts it. Since version 7.40, REAPER includes a professional two-lane crossfade editor, similar in spirit to the ones in the specialist classical editing systems. It is the natural next step after an S-D edit: ReaEdit puts a crossfade at each join, and the crossfade editor lets you listen to it closely and fine-tune where it falls. It is part of REAPER itself, so it is there whether or not you use ReaEdit.

Opening it Select the right-hand item of the crossfade you want to look at, then run ReaEdit's Crossfade Editor action. To find it, open the Action List (Actions > Show action list...) and search for ReaEdit_Crossfade Editor. Bind a shortcut to it, since you will use it often: F is a good choice, and it is easy to reach with the other editing keys. Run the action again to close the window. The action turns on ripple per track while the editor is open. If the selected item is not the right-hand item of a crossfade, it tells you so and does nothing. It needs REAPER 7.40 or later, the version that introduced the two-lane editor.

What you see Two lanes. The top lane shows the item on the left of the join (the one leaving the crossfade) and the bottom lane shows the item on the right (the one entering it). Ghost waveforms. Each item's audio carries on past the crossfade, shown dimmed, so you can see the material that is normally hidden. This is what makes it possible to line up transients by eye and place the crossfade just before one. The crossfade itself. The two white vertical lines mark where the crossfade starts and ends, and the red curves show the fade-out of the left item and the fade-in of the right item. Phase alignment. The percentage at the top of the window shows how well the two items currently match in phase. Item names and time. The names of the two items appear in the top corners, and a time ruler runs along the bottom.

The controls The top row of the window holds the settings for the crossfade: Arrow buttons move around the crossfade and its neighbours Link fade-in/fade-out edits makes changes to one fade apply to the other Lock left-hand start keeps the start of the left-hand item where it is while you adjust the join Crossfade length sets the length of the crossfade (type a value, and choose the units from the list beside it) Phase align tries to line the two items up for the best phase match Re-center brings the crossfade back to the middle of the window after you have scrolled or zoomed The bottom row is for listening: Play, pause, stop and loop audition the crossfade, with the Pre-roll and Post-roll boxes setting how much audio is played before and after it Solo crossfaded items plays only the items involved in the crossfade Mute Left and Mute Right silence one side so you can hear the other on its own Snapshots, Presets and Options store and recall settings and change how the editor behaves You can also work directly in the two lanes with the mouse to move the crossfade and shape the curves. Tip Audition the left and right items on their own (with Mute Left and Mute Right) before you judge the crossfade. A problem you can hear in one item alone will not be cured by changing the crossfade length.

More detail REAPER's own user guide describes every control and mouse gesture in the crossfade editor, including the phase alignment and view options that this page only mentions. ReaEdit does not add keyboard shortcuts to it; the window uses REAPER's own.

Source-destination editing can span two open project tabs: the source material in one, the performance you are assembling in the other. This is useful for keeping each take, or each movement, in its own project.

Project markers Two extra markers say which tab is which: Marker Name Action Destination project DEST PROJECT Set Dest Project Marker Source project SOURCE PROJECT Set Source Project Marker Place each at the edit cursor in its tab. The position does not matter; the beginning or the very end of the timeline is a good place to keep them out of the way. Like the other markers there is only ever one of each.

Working across tabs Set DEST PROJECT in the destination tab and SOURCE PROJECT in the source tab. Place the destination markers in the destination tab and the source markers in the source tab, as usual. Run S-D Edit (or any of the other edit actions). The one rule is that source markers must be paired with a source project marker, and destination markers with a destination project marker. Your markers stay in place in both tabs after an edit, which makes it quick to undo in the destination tab and apply the same edit again. If you have set only one project marker you will see "Only one S-D project marker was found. Use zero for regular single project S-D editing or use two for multi-tab S-D editing." If markers and project markers do not match, you will be told they should be paired. Remove the project markers with Delete S-D Project Markers when you have finished.

ReaEdit is built to be used with OSARA, the free accessibility extension for REAPER, and if you are blind or low-vision you should install it (see the Accessibility FAQ for how). OSARA is what makes ReaEdit speak the result of every action, and the keyboard crossfade mode needs it. If you work visually you do not need OSARA at all: ReaEdit works fully without it, shows messages in ordinary dialogs where it needs to say something, and the Crossfade Editor action opens REAPER's own visual crossfade editor.

What is spoken Marker actions announce what they placed and where, for example "Added source out @ 1 minute 23 seconds" S-D Edit and the other edits announce "S-D edit complete", and tell you if a crossfade was shortened or slivers were removed Delete All S-D markers and Delete S-D Project Markers confirm what they removed Warnings that would otherwise appear in a dialog are spoken instead, so you are not interrupted

Marker order checks When OSARA is installed, ReaEdit also guards against placing a marker on the wrong side of its partner. If you place destination IN after the existing destination OUT, it deletes the stale destination OUT and says so; if you try to place source OUT before the existing source IN, it tells you "Source out must be after source in." and does not place it. This means an edit can never silently take far more material than you intended. Without OSARA these checks are not made.

A suggested way to work Bind the marker actions to keys you can reach without looking (see Keyboard Shortcuts). Navigate to a point with REAPER's normal navigation and listen to where you are. Place the marker and listen for the confirmation. Make the edit and listen across the join.

Crossfades REAPER's crossfade editor is visual, and at the moment it is not fully accessible with a screen reader, so ReaEdit includes its own keyboard-driven crossfade mode for use with OSARA. It has full parity with the visual editor in the features classical music engineers use (slipping, nudging, shifting, widening and narrowing the crossfade, shaping the fades, auditioning each side and reverting), driven entirely from the keyboard, and it speaks everything it does. It needs one-time setup, described in that chapter.

Beyond ReaEdit ReaEdit covers source-destination editing and crossfades. ReaClassical provides a full accessibility experience across the board: it is designed so that a blind or low-vision engineer can carry out a complete classical production, from creating a project through recording, importing, editing, mixing, mastering and rendering, using only the keyboard and a screen reader. It does this with its own screen reader bridge, Clara (for Windows and macOS), accessible windows, keyboard modes and a Terminal. See Using ReaClassical with a Screen Reader in the ReaClassical manual.

ReaEdit includes a keyboard-driven crossfade mode. It gives you the same control over a crossfade as REAPER's two-lane crossfade editor, but entirely from the keyboard, with every action spoken. It is designed for screen reader users, and it needs OSARA to be installed, because OSARA is what speaks. If you work visually, you do not need it: use REAPER's own crossfade editor.

Why it exists REAPER's own crossfade editor is visual: you read the waveforms and drag them with the mouse. At the moment it is not fully accessible with a screen reader, so ReaEdit includes its own keyboard version, with full parity with the visual editor in the features classical music engineers use: moving the crossfade and the audio inside it, widening and narrowing it, shaping the fades, listening to each side, and putting everything back. It is driven entirely from the keyboard and every action is spoken, so you never need to see the window. REAPER's editor has a few further features that are not part of the keyboard mode: view options, which do not apply without sight, phase alignment, which classical editing does not call for, and presets. With and without OSARA The same action starts both. With OSARA installed it starts crossfade mode. Without OSARA it opens REAPER's own visual crossfade editor instead, as described in REAPER's Crossfade Editor.

Setting it up You do this once. Bind a key to the Crossfade Editor action. Open the Action List (Actions > Show action list...), search for ReaEdit_Crossfade Editor and give it a shortcut. ReaEdit does not choose this key for you, so use whichever suits you; F is a suggestion, and it is what ReaClassical uses. Create the key file. The first time you use that key with OSARA running, ReaEdit tells you the crossfade mode keys are not installed yet and offers to create them. Choose Yes. It adds the crossfade mode's actions to your Action List, which ReaPack does not do for you, writes a file called ReaEdit Crossfade Mode.ReaperKeyMap into REAPER's KeyMaps folder, and tells you where it is. Import the file. In the Action List choose Import/export, then Import shortcuts/custom actions, import all sections..., and open the file. That is all. If you choose No at the prompt, crossfade mode starts anyway and you are asked again next time until the keys are installed; choose Cancel to do nothing for now. ReaEdit uses the last alternate keyboard section, Main (alt-16) The crossfade mode keys are set in REAPER's last alternate keyboard section, Main (alt-16), and importing the key file sets shortcuts in that section. Very few people use it, but if you have set up shortcuts of your own there, please back them up first. In the Action List choose the section Main (alt-16), then Import/export, then Export shortcuts/custom actions for this section only..., and save the file somewhere safe. Importing the key file may replace shortcuts you already have on the same keys. It does not change your main keymap or any other section. The keys only exist while crossfade mode is on. REAPER switches to that section when the mode starts and switches back from it when it ends, so they never touch your normal shortcuts and nothing you have bound in the main section changes. While the mode is on, REAPER's own standard shortcuts are switched off as well, so a stray key press cannot trigger something unexpected (such as deleting the selected items).

Using it Select the right-hand item of a crossfade. Or use the actions Navigate to Next Crossfade and Navigate to Previous Crossfade, which jump to a crossfade, select its right-hand item and say which one it is, for example "Crossfade 2 of 5 at 19 seconds, 950 milliseconds, take 3 to take 4, 100 milliseconds". You can bind keys to them (Alt+W and Alt+Q are suggested). Press the key you bound to Crossfade Editor. You hear "Crossfade mode on". ReaEdit selects both items of the crossfade and their matching items on every track, puts the edit cursor at the centre of the crossfade, and switches on ripple per track for as long as the mode is on. Use the keys below. Every action says what it did. Press Esc to leave. Inside the mode Esc always leaves it, whichever key you used to start it. You hear "Crossfade mode off", and your ripple setting is put back as it was. If nothing is selected you hear "No items selected", and if the selected item is not the right-hand item of a crossfade you hear "No crossfade to the left of this item". The mode does not start.

h: Which side you are working on
x: Which side you are working on Most actions work on the selected side of the crossfade: the left item, the right item, or both. You start with both selected. Choose with S (left), D (right) and A (both), and press Alt+A to hear which side is selected and the names of the items. A few actions need a single side and tell you if both are selected: slipping, nudging and changing an item's volume. Where an action behaves differently for the left item, the right item and both, the key table above says what it does to the selected side.

Step sizes Slipping, nudging, shifting, widening, narrowing and changing the fades all move by the same amount, 5 milliseconds to begin with. The "larger step" version of the same key moves by 5 times that. Change both in ReaEdit's Preferences: XFM nudge (ms) and XFM x modifier multiplier.
The keys

Choosing what to work on Key What it does Larger step A Select both items of the crossfade S Select the left item D Select the right item Alt+A Say which side is selected and the names of the items Q Go to the previous crossfade (the mode follows you) W Go to the next crossfade (the mode follows you)

Listening Key What it does Larger step Z Play 1.5 seconds either side of the crossfade centre (3 seconds with the larger step) Ctrl+Z or Shift+Z X Play the left item up to the crossfade centre Ctrl+X or Shift+X C Play the right item from the crossfade centre Ctrl+C or Shift+C

Moving the audio Key What it does Larger step ← Slip the selected item's audio left (material after the crossfade moves with it) Shift+← → Slip the selected item's audio right Shift+→ Ctrl+← Nudge the selected item left Ctrl+Shift+← Ctrl+→ Nudge the selected item right Ctrl+Shift+→

Moving the crossfade Key What it does Larger step J Shift the crossfade left (nothing after it moves) Ctrl+J or Shift+J K Shift the crossfade right Ctrl+K or Shift+K I Widen the crossfade Ctrl+I or Shift+I U Narrow the crossfade Ctrl+U or Shift+U

Fades Key What it does Larger step P Grow the start of the fade (start it earlier) Ctrl+P O Shrink the start of the fade Ctrl+O ] Grow the end of the fade Ctrl+[ [ Shrink the end of the fade Ctrl+] T Cycle the fade shape N Match the right item's fade-in to the left item's fade-out M Match the left item's fade-out to the right item's fade-in

Level Key What it does Larger step ↑ Raise the selected item's volume by 1 dB ↓ Lower the selected item's volume by 1 dB Ctrl+↑ Raise the selected item's volume by 0.2 dB Ctrl+↓ Lower the selected item's volume by 0.2 dB Ctrl+0 Reset the selected item's volume

Resetting and undoing Key What it does Larger step 0 Reset both fades to an equal-power crossfade of your S-D crossfade length Ctrl+Alt+0 Put the crossfade back as it was when you first changed it in this session
Playback, saving and leaving Key What it does Larger step Space Play or stop Ctrl+S Save the project Esc Leave crossfade mode

Tips Audition before you judge. Z plays either side of the crossfade, and X and C let you hear the left and right items on their own. Change one thing at a time and listen. If a change makes it worse, Revert (Ctrl+Alt+0) puts the crossfade back as it was when you first changed it, however many steps ago that was. When a move would use up too much of a neighbouring item, the action refuses and says why ("Cannot slip: right item's post-fade content too short"). Nothing has changed when you hear that. Everything works on all your tracks together, as ReaEdit's edits do, so the tracks stay in step. Undo works as normal. Each action is a single undo step.

If it does not work The keys do nothing. The key file has not been imported. See Setting it up. If you chose No at the prompt, use the Crossfade Editor key again and choose Yes, then import the file. The crossfade editor opens instead of crossfade mode. OSARA was not detected. Check that it is installed and loaded; the Accessibility FAQ links to its official installation instructions. "No crossfade to the left of this item". Select the right-hand item of the crossfade.

OSARA and your screen reader Do I need OSARA? If you are blind or low-vision, yes: OSARA is what makes ReaEdit speak, and the keyboard crossfade mode only starts when OSARA is installed. If you work visually you do not need it, and there is no reason to install it: the markers, edits and deletes work fully without it, messages appear in ordinary dialogs, and the Crossfade Editor action opens REAPER's own visual crossfade editor, which suits you better. How do I install OSARA? OSARA is a free accessibility extension for REAPER, installed separately from ReaEdit. Download it, and follow its installation instructions, from the official OSARA website. The REAPER accessibility wiki has more guidance on setting up REAPER with a screen reader, and OSARA's own project page is on GitHub. Restart REAPER after installing. ReaEdit finds OSARA by itself: to check, select the right-hand item of a crossfade and run the Crossfade Editor action. If you hear "Crossfade mode on", OSARA is working with ReaEdit. I use ReaClassical. Do I need OSARA? No. ReaClassical has its own screen reader bridge, Clara, which speaks everything ReaClassical does and takes the place of OSARA in a ReaClassical install (installing Clara removes any OSARA plugin, and it is installed with a single Terminal command). See Using ReaClassical with a Screen Reader in the ReaClassical manual. ReaEdit is for people who use REAPER without ReaClassical, and OSARA is what makes it speak there. What does ReaClassical add for blind and low-vision engineers? A full accessibility experience across the whole production. ReaClassical is designed so that you can carry out a complete classical production, from creating a project through recording, importing, editing, mixing, mastering and rendering, using only the keyboard and a screen reader. ReaEdit gives you the source-destination editing and the crossfade mode; ReaClassical adds accessible versions of its windows, keyboard modes for crossfades, items and the mixer, a Terminal, and guides for every stage of the workflow. See Using ReaClassical with a Screen Reader in the ReaClassical manual.

The keyboard crossfade mode Why does ReaEdit have its own crossfade mode? REAPER's own crossfade editor is visual, and at the moment it is not fully accessible with a screen reader. The keyboard crossfade mode has full parity with the visual editor in the features classical music engineers use, is driven entirely from the keyboard, and speaks every step. See Crossfade Mode (Keyboard). The crossfade mode keys do nothing. The key file has not been imported yet. See Crossfade Mode (Keyboard). Will the crossfade mode change my shortcuts? Only in one place. ReaEdit puts the crossfade mode keys in REAPER's last alternate keyboard section, Main (alt-16), and nowhere else: your main keymap and the other sections are not touched. Very few people use alt-16, but if you have shortcuts of your own there, back them up before importing the key file, because the import may replace shortcuts on the same keys. The Crossfade Mode (Keyboard) chapter shows how to export that section first. The crossfade editor opens instead of crossfade mode. OSARA was not detected. Check that it is installed and loaded, and see How do I install OSARA? above.

Crossfade mode messages "No items selected" or "No crossfade to the left of this item" Crossfade mode starts from the right-hand item of a crossfade. Select it, or use Navigate to Next Crossfade, and try again. See Crossfade Mode (Keyboard). "Select left or right item first" The action needs one side. Press S for the left item or D for the right item. "Slip requires single item selected" Slipping works on one item at a time. Choose a side with S or D. "Cannot slip", "Cannot nudge", "Cannot narrow" or "Cannot shrink", followed by a reason The move would use up too much of a neighbouring item, so ReaEdit refused and nothing changed. Use a smaller step, or move something else first. "No next crossfade", "No previous crossfade" or "No crossfades on this track" You are at the last or first crossfade, or the track has none. "No crossfade context" Crossfade mode has lost track of which crossfade it was on, usually because the items were changed outside the mode. Leave the mode and start it again.
ReaEdit does not assign keyboard shortcuts, so that it can never clash with your own. Because you will place markers and make edits constantly, set up keys before you start serious work.

Binding a key Open the Action List (Actions > Show action list...). Search for ReaEdit and select an action. Click Add... under Shortcuts for selected action, press the key you want and confirm. REAPER warns you if the key is already used.

Suggested keys These are the keys ReaClassical uses, so they will feel familiar if you move between the two. Check REAPER's conflict warning for each one. Action Suggested key Add Destination IN marker 1 Add Destination OUT Marker 2 Add Source IN marker 3 Add Source OUT marker 4 S-D Edit 5 3-point Insert Edit F3 Insert with timestretching F4 Delete With Ripple Backspace Delete Leaving Silence Ctrl+Backspace Delete All S-D markers Ctrl+Delete Set Dest Project Marker Ctrl+Alt+1 (or Ctrl+Alt+2) Set Source Project Marker Ctrl+Alt+3 (or Ctrl+Alt+4) Delete S-D Project Markers Shift+Delete Preferences F5 Crossfade Editor F Navigate to Next Crossfade Alt+W Navigate to Previous Crossfade Alt+Q The Crossfade Editor action opens REAPER's crossfade editor, or with OSARA starts the keyboard crossfade mode. The crossfade mode's own keys are separate: they are set up for you and only work while the mode is on, so you do not bind them yourself. The first four sit under one hand on the number row and read left to right the way an edit is described: destination in and out, then source in and out. Pick whatever suits you; the actions do not care. Mouse and toolbar You can also put the actions on a REAPER toolbar or in a menu through REAPER's own customisation, or run them from the Action List.
The ReaEdit actions you use directly, as they appear in the Action List (search for ReaEdit). In the list each name begins with "Script: ".

Markers Action What it does ReaEdit_Add Destination IN marker Places DEST-IN at the edit cursor (or play position) ReaEdit_Add Destination OUT Marker Places DEST-OUT ReaEdit_Add Source IN marker Places SOURCE-IN ReaEdit_Add Source OUT marker Places SOURCE-OUT ReaEdit_Set Dest Project Marker Places DEST PROJECT for editing between tabs ReaEdit_Set Source Project Marker Places SOURCE PROJECT for editing between tabs ReaEdit_Delete All S-D markers Removes the four S-D markers from every open project ReaEdit_Delete S-D Project Markers Removes the two project-tab markers

Edits Action What it does ReaEdit_S-D Edit The 2-, 3- or 4-point source-destination edit, with crossfades ReaEdit_3-point Insert Edit Assembly-line insert: source passage inserted at destination IN ReaEdit_Insert with timestretching 4-point edit with the source stretched to fit the destination
Deleting Action What it does ReaEdit_Delete With Ripple Removes the source passage and closes the gap with a crossfade ReaEdit_Delete Leaving Silence Removes the source passage and leaves the gap

Crossfades Action What it does ReaEdit_Crossfade Editor Opens REAPER's crossfade editor, or with OSARA starts or leaves the keyboard crossfade mode ReaEdit_Navigate to Next Crossfade Goes to the next crossfade, selects its right-hand item and says which one it is ReaEdit_Navigate to Previous Crossfade The same, going backwards ReaEdit_XFM ... The 45 actions that make up the keyboard crossfade mode. ReaPack installs them but does not list them in the Action List; setting up the crossfade mode keys adds them (OSARA users only). They are bound for you and only work inside the mode: see Crossfade Mode (Keyboard)
Settings Action What it does ReaEdit_Preferences The S-D crossfade length (ms, default 35), and for the crossfade mode the nudge (ms, default 5) and the larger-step multiplier (default 5)

Messages and what they mean "Please add at least 2 valid source-destination markers" S-D Edit needs at least one destination marker and one source marker. See Edit Types. "Please add 3 valid source-destination markers: DEST-IN, SOURCE-IN and SOURCE-OUT" 3-point Insert Edit needs exactly those three markers. "Please use SOURCE-IN and SOURCE-OUT markers" The delete actions take their range from the source markers. See Deleting. "Please make sure there is material to copy between your source markers" The source range is empty, or contains no items. Check the source markers and that the tracks have material there. "Only one S-D project marker was found" Use no project markers for editing in a single project, or two (one in each tab) for editing between tabs. See Editing Between Project Tabs. "Source or destination markers should be paired with the corresponding source or destination project marker" In a cross-tab edit, the source markers must be in the tab with the source project marker and the destination markers in the tab with the destination project marker. "The DEST-IN marker has been moved since the last assembly line edit" You moved destination IN after the previous assembly-line insert. Answer Yes to start a new sequence, No to put the marker back at the previous item's edge. "Crossfade shortened to N ms ... due to limited source material" There was not enough source material for a full crossfade at that join. Move the marker further into the take if you want the full length.

Frequently asked questions Questions about OSARA, screen readers and the keyboard crossfade mode are in the Accessibility FAQ. I installed ReaEdit but see no actions. Search the Action List for ReaEdit. If you installed from the zip, you must run Register ReaEdit actions.lua once. If you used ReaPack, run Extensions > ReaPack > Synchronize packages and check ReaEdit is installed in Browse packages. How is this different from ReaClassical? ReaEdit is only the source-destination editing part of ReaClassical, for people who want it in their own REAPER. ReaClassical takes a classical production from start to finish: An easy Create Project workflow, with a choice of horizontal or vertical workflow approaches, and project management through a dedicated Mission Control window Robust zero-collision recording with the Record Panel: automatic take numbering, session naming, rankings and notes, scheduled recording and more Smart importing Editing: everything in ReaEdit, plus healing edits, finding takes, source auditioning, automatic crossfade protection, razor editing and many more functions Mixing with a unique approach to automation: mixer snapshot scenes (faders, pan, mute, solo, FX, sends and routing) that are recalled automatically during playback and converted to real automation before rendering. Everyday automation is just as easy: select a passage, set the level and optional ramps in and out, and ReaClassical creates the automation for you, with no need to add automation points by hand Mastering that is unique in the DAW world: all your album and CD-Text metadata in one window, with the CUE file, CD-Text and HTML album report updating automatically, a DDP image a click away, and no need to keep album markers and items in sync by hand Quick rendering from the metadata editor: one click to WAV, FLAC, Opus, MP3 or a DDP image, without REAPER's render dialog In all, ReaClassical has nearly 300 actions. Because ReaClassical already includes all of ReaEdit's functions, if you use ReaClassical you do not need ReaEdit. If you use a screen reader, ReaClassical has its own screen reader bridge, Clara, so OSARA is not needed with ReaClassical (see the Accessibility FAQ). See reaclassical.com. I love ReaEdit! How do I move up to ReaClassical? ReaClassical is free and open source, so there is nothing to buy. See reaclassical.com for what it includes. Install it. Run the ReaClassical installer for your system. It creates a separate, self-contained ReaClassical folder with its own REAPER, so your existing REAPER and ReaEdit are left untouched. ReaClassical cannot be installed into an existing REAPER. See Installation in the ReaClassical manual. Keep your keys. ReaClassical's marker and edit keys are the ones this manual suggests (1 to 4 for the markers, 5 for the S-D edit), so your hands already know them. Bring your work across. A ReaEdit project is an ordinary REAPER project, and ReaClassical can convert an existing one. See Converting a Standard REAPER Project. Do not install ReaEdit into your ReaClassical instance: it already has all of these functions, and many more. Do I need a licence or an account? No. ReaEdit is free to use. Does it work with my existing projects? Yes. It works on any project; there is nothing to convert. A project edited with ReaEdit is an ordinary REAPER project that opens in any REAPER, whether or not ReaEdit is installed. Why did the edit change all my tracks? ReaEdit treats the tracks of a project as parallel channels of one recording and edits them together. Keep material that should not be edited together in a separate project.

The community forum The ReaClassical subforum of the REAPER forum is the place to ask questions, report bugs and request features for these editing functions. Please say which version of ReaEdit and REAPER you are using. In REAPER you can find ReaEdit's version in Extensions > ReaPack > Manage repositories... or in Browse packages.
Support ReaEdit is free, and the forum is the only place to get help with it; there is no official support beyond that.
